subject: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA

messages.author: 220fa9504682ce10
messages.subject: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
parts:
Hi all,

I am dealing with MSI-data for the first time, and have been playing with a dataset, trying out different software packages. I ran Matlab's PCA algorithm on my data processed with MSiReader, and then tried out the processing and PCA in Cardinal for comparison, getting vastly different results.  I realised that the default in Cardinal is not to z-standardize the data for the PCA, whilst this is something that is generally done in my field and which I did when running the Matlab algorithm. Turning on z-standardization in Cardinal then gave me very similar results to the Matlab PCA. In my understanding, if the data are not z-standardized, the peaks with the highest mean intensity will contribute and explain more variance in the data, is this correct? It seems to be the case for my data: with the Cardinal PCA, the highest intensity peaks also have the highest standard deviation and have the strongest loadings on component 1 and there seems to be linear relationship between average peak height and component loading. So I was wondering if anybody could explain to me what is the rationale behind not z-standardizing the data. Is it that the highest peaks are likely the least noisy peaks? Or that in order to interpret the basis spectra (component spectra) better, it is better to keep the original scaling of the data? The thing I am concerned about is that if doing so, I will miss peaks that are not amongst the highest, but that are spatially very informative. I’d be grateful if I could get some input on this!

Thanks a lot,

Ilona

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: To z-standardize or not to z-standardize data for PCA
parts:
You are essentially correct. When you don't standardize/scale the data beforehand, PCA will be dominated by the peaks with the highest variance. This is not necessarily the ones with the highest mean intensities, but that is often the case (particularly because MS data tends to have multiplicative variance, so higher intensity peaks will usually have higher variance). This isn't necessarily undesirable, depending on whether or not you think the peaks with the highest variance will also be the most relevant.

It is essentially up to you whether to scale the data, and there is no issue with looking at both scaled and unscaled results. If you believe there may be peaks with lower intensity/variance that may contribute to whatever you are investigating, then you are correct that it would be better to scale the data.

My reasoning behind the defaults here is primarily to be consistent with other PCA implementations elsewhere in R such as the prcomp() function.

-Kylie
